lessons.title: Light, heat and sound
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III — Elementary Science and Technology; to be checked against the official texts
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain why shadows form and tell transparent, translucent and opaque materials apart.
Describe how heat moves and name good conductors and insulators of heat.
Explain that sound is made by vibrations and travels through materials.
reviewNotes: Standard textbook facts only; temperature of boiling/freezing and speeds of light and sound are deliberately left out.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Light
blocks.md: We see things when light from a **source** (the sun, a lamp, a fire) or **reflected** by an object (like the moon) enters our eyes. **Light travels in straight lines.** **Transparent** materials let light through (clear glass, clean water). **Translucent** ones let some light through (frosted glass, tissue paper). **Opaque** ones block light (wood, metal). A **shadow** forms when an opaque object blocks light.

blocks.caption: A shadow forms behind an opaque object.
blocks.alt: A lamp on the left sends three rays to the right. A grey object blocks the rays. Behind it there is a grey shadow.

blocks.title: Heat
blocks.md: **Heat** moves from a **hotter** place to a **colder** one. In **solids** (metals) it moves by conduction: a metal spoon in hot tea becomes hot. In **liquids and air** hot parts rise (convection). The **sun's heat** reaches us across space (radiation). **Conductors** (metals) let heat pass easily; **insulators** (wood, plastic, cloth) do not. Temperature is measured with a thermometer in **degrees Celsius (°C)**.

blocks.title: Sound
blocks.md: **Sound** is made when things **vibrate** (move quickly to and fro): a drum skin, a guitar string, our vocal cords. Sound travels through air, water and solids, but **not through empty space**. A **high pitch** comes from fast vibrations, a **loud** sound from big vibrations. An **echo** is sound that bounces off a hard surface. Light travels much faster than sound, so we see lightning before we hear thunder.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying that a metal pot handle is made of metal because it is a good **insulator**: metal is a conductor, so handles are made of wood or plastic.
- Saying that the moon is a source of light: it **reflects** the sun's light.
- Saying that sound needs no material to travel through.
- Looking at the sun directly or with sunglasses only: it can damage the eyes.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Why do cooking pots have handles of wood or plastic?
steps: The metal of the pot is a good conductor, so the heat travels to the handle.
Wood and plastic are insulators, so the handle stays cool and we can hold it.
blocks.answer: Because wood and plastic are insulators: they do not let the heat pass, so the handle stays cool.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: You see lightning and hear thunder a few seconds later. Why?
steps: Light travels much faster than sound.
The light reaches us almost at once; the sound takes longer.

lessons.title: Magnets, forces and simple machines
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III — Elementary Science and Technology; to be checked against the official texts
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Say which materials a magnet attracts and what poles do.
Describe push and pull forces, friction and gravity.
Name simple machines and say how they make work easier.
reviewNotes: Weight vs mass is only mentioned; unit of force (newton) is not covered. Check whether gravity/friction are in the Class 6 syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Magnets
blocks.md: A **magnet** attracts objects made of **iron** and **steel** (they are called **magnetic**). It does not attract wood, plastic, glass or most other metals such as copper and aluminium. A magnet has two **poles**, **north** and **south**. **Unlike poles attract** (north and south). **Like poles repel** (north and north push apart).

blocks.title: Forces
blocks.md: A **force** is a push or a pull. A force can start or stop an object, make it go faster or slower, change its direction or change its shape. **Gravity** pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth: it makes things fall and gives them **weight**. **Friction** is a force that slows moving things when two surfaces rub. It is useful for brakes and for walking, but it wears machines, so oil is used to reduce it.

blocks.caption: A lever: a small effort on one side lifts a load on the other.
blocks.alt: A long bar rests on a triangle called the pivot. A blue load sits on the left end. A red arrow pushes down on the right end.

blocks.title: Simple machines
blocks.md: A **simple machine** makes work easier (less effort, or a better direction). Examples: **lever** (see-saw, scissors, wheelbarrow, crowbar), **pulley** (raising water from a well, a flag), **inclined plane** (a ramp or a sloping road), **wheel and axle** (bicycle, cart), **wedge** (axe, knife) and **screw** (a bottle top, a jack).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying that a magnet attracts all metals. Only some metals (iron, steel) are magnetic.
- Saying that like poles attract.
- Believing that a machine **creates** energy: it only makes the work easier.
- Mixing up weight (a force, from gravity) and mass (how much matter).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: A magnet is held near a nail, a coin made of copper, and a plastic ruler. Which will it attract?
steps: The nail is made of iron (or steel): magnetic.
Copper and plastic are not magnetic.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Why is it easier to push a heavy barrel up a ramp than to lift it?
steps: A ramp is an inclined plane: it spreads the work over a longer distance.
We need a smaller force, but we must push over a longer distance.
blocks.answer: A ramp (inclined plane) needs a smaller force, but over a longer distance.

lessons.title: Electricity and electrical safety
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III — Elementary Science and Technology; to be checked against the official texts
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe a simple electric circuit and what a switch does.
Tell conductors from insulators of electricity.
Follow the safety rules for electricity.
reviewNotes: The existing 'Matter and energy' lesson also covers simple circuits; this lesson stresses conductors, insulators and safety. Safety rules are generic and should be reviewed by a qualified person (e.g. an electrician or teacher).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: A simple circuit
blocks.md: A **circuit** is a closed path for electricity. A simple circuit has a **cell** (or battery) that pushes the electricity, **wires** and a **bulb**. A **switch** opens or closes the path: when the switch is **closed** the bulb lights; when it is **open** the circuit is broken and the bulb goes out.

blocks.caption: A simple circuit with a cell, a bulb and a switch.
blocks.alt: A rectangle of wire. On the left side there is a cell. At the top is a bulb. At the bottom is a switch.

blocks.title: Conductors and insulators
blocks.md: **Conductors** let electricity pass: copper, iron, aluminium and other metals. **Insulators** do not: plastic, rubber, dry wood, glass and cloth. Wires are made of metal (conductor) covered with plastic (insulator). **Water that is not pure** and the **human body** also conduct electricity, so they are dangerous near electricity.

blocks.title: Safety rules
blocks.md:
- Never touch bare wires, sockets or switches with **wet hands**.
- Never put fingers, pins or metal into a socket.
- Do not play with electric wires, and **stay away from fallen power lines**: tell an adult at once.
- Do not fly kites near power lines or climb electricity poles.
- Do not plug too many things into one socket.
- Let an adult unplug broken equipment. During a storm, stay inside and do not shelter under a tall tree.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Thinking a bulb lights with only one wire connected: the circuit must be a **complete loop**.
- Using a pin or knife to take out a plug.
- Saying that all metals are magnetic or that all materials conduct: plastic and rubber are insulators.
- Using a damaged cable because it 'still works'.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: A bulb does not light in a circuit with a cell, wires and a switch. Give two possible reasons.
steps: The switch is open, so the circuit is not complete.
A wire is loose or broken, or the cell is flat.
blocks.answer: The switch may be open, or a wire may be loose or the cell flat.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Why are electric wires covered with plastic?
steps: The wire inside is metal and carries the electricity.
Plastic is an insulator, so it protects us from the electricity.
blocks.answer: Plastic is an insulator, so it protects us from shock.
